title: Does HCF times LCM equal the product for three numbers?
description: The rule for two numbers is tested on four, six and ten. The highest common factor times the lowest common multiple is one hundred twenty, but the product is two hundred forty, so the rule does not hold for three numbers. Keeko expects the rule to work because it worked for two numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: a rule found for two numbers must be tested again for three numbers, and here it fails. Watch for students who expect the rule to carry over to three numbers.

source: Does HCF × LCM equal the product for three numbers? Test 4, 6 and 10.
video_script.why: The child knows the rule for two numbers and now tests whether it holds for three numbers.
video_script.substitution: Break the numbers into primes, find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple, and compare their product with the product of the three numbers.
video_script.anchor: The numbers four, six and ten with their prime factors written in a column.
video_script.wrong_answer: the rule works for three numbers too
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko expects the rule to work for three numbers because it worked for two, but one hundred twenty is not two hundred forty.
video_script.payoff_line: No, the rule does not hold for three numbers

final_answer.value: No: for 4, 6 and 10, HCF × LCM is 120 but the product is 240
final_answer.spoken: no, for four, six and ten, the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple is one hundred twenty but the product is two hundred forty

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We take three numbers, four, six and ten.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The largest number that divides all three is called their highest common factor.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The smallest number that is a multiple of all three is called their lowest common multiple.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Does the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple equal the product, as for two numbers?

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

marks.m2: a balance appears with a calculation on each side

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Every number can be broken into primes, which are numbers whose only factors are one and itself.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>To test a rule, we work out both sides and compare them.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

beats.on_screen: To find: whether HCF × LCM equals the product 4 × 6 × 10

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to test whether the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple equals the product.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, break each number into primes. Four is two times two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six is two times three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Ten is two times five.

marks.m1: the 2 in all three numbers is lit as the HCF

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, only the prime two is in all three numbers, so the highest common factor is two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The lowest common multiple needs two twos, one three and one five. That is two times two times three times five, which is sixty.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple is two times sixty. That is one hundred twenty.

marks.m2: 120 and 240 are set side by side with a not-equal sign

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, the product is four times six times ten. Four times six is twenty four, and twenty four times ten is two hundred forty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred twenty and two hundred forty are not the same.

beats.on_screen: Answer: No: for 4, 6 and 10, HCF × LCM is 120 but the product is 240

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>No, the rule does not hold for three numbers.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For four, six and ten, the two multiplied give one hundred twenty. The product is two hundred forty.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

marks.m3: the column of 2s is lit with counts 2, 1 and 1

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the rule works for three numbers too, because it worked for two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But one hundred twenty is only half of two hundred forty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Look at the prime two. Its counts are two, one and one.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The product uses all four twos. The highest common factor and the lowest common multiple use only three.
